questions.stem: A marketing team has used Claude for six weeks to draft product descriptions. Drafting time per description fell sharply, but every draft still goes through an editor who checks claims and brand tone. In a budget meeting, the VP of marketing asks the team lead directly: 'So can we let our three freelance copywriters go at the end of the quarter?' What is the MOST appropriate way for the team lead to answer?

options.text: Say yes, since the pilot shows Claude now produces the drafts much faster than the freelancers did, so their capacity is no longer needed.
Say that the pilot says nothing useful about staffing, and decline to answer until the company sets an official policy on AI and headcount.
Share the measured time saved and the editing still required, explain which work still needs people, and offer to model capacity before any decision.
Ask Claude to estimate how many writers the team needs from now on, and present that number to the VP as the recommendation for the quarter.

questions.explanation: The VP is asking a business question that the pilot only partly answers. The pilot measured **drafting time**, but every draft still needs an editor, and the freelancers may also do work the pilot never touched (research, interviews, final polish). An honest answer gives the evidence that exists, names the work that still needs people, and offers a proper capacity analysis before anyone makes a staffing decision. That keeps the value story credible without overpromising.

whyWrong.A: This turns a drafting-speed result into a staffing promise. The pilot did not measure whether the editing load, quality checks and other freelance work could be absorbed, so the claim overstates what the evidence shows.
whyWrong.B: Declining to engage treats a fair business question as forbidden. Pilot evidence is a relevant input to resourcing decisions — the problem is overinterpreting it, not mentioning it.
whyWrong.D: A model-generated headcount number is not evidence. Claude does not know the team's full workload, and presenting its estimate as the recommendation hands a people decision to an unverified output.

questions.mindset: Report what the pilot actually measured; don't stretch a speed result into a promise it can't support.

questions.stem: A consulting firm now uses Claude to help prepare first drafts of client market reports, and a consultant reviews and fact-checks each one. A sales director wants to add this line to the firm's pitch deck: 'Our AI-powered reports are error-free and delivered in half the time.' Which revision BEST communicates the value honestly to prospective clients?

options.text: 'AI helps our consultants draft faster; every report is reviewed and fact-checked by a named consultant before it reaches you.'
'Our reports are produced by advanced AI, which is the most accurate way to analyze markets that is currently available.'
'Our AI-powered reports are error-free and delivered in half the time, with an optional human review if you request it.'
'We do not mention AI in our process, so clients judge our reports on their quality alone rather than on the tools we use.'

questions.explanation: Claude can produce incorrect or misleading content, which is why the firm reviews every draft. A claim of 'error-free' cannot be supported and would damage trust the first time a mistake surfaced. The honest version still sells real value (faster drafting) and makes the **human review** the guarantee, which is both true and reassuring to clients.

whyWrong.B: This swaps one overclaim for another. Calling AI 'the most accurate way' to analyze markets is unsupported, and it hides the consultant review that actually protects quality.
whyWrong.C: It keeps the false 'error-free' promise and makes review optional, which is the reverse of the firm's real process and of what makes the output trustworthy.
whyWrong.D: Hiding AI use can conflict with contracts, policies or client expectations, and it gives up a genuine value point. Honesty about the process is the safer and stronger message.

questions.mindset: Sell the real benefit and let human review be the quality promise; never claim 'error-free'.

questions.stem: An operations lead wants approval to use Claude for summarizing internal supplier-performance reports. Before signing off, the company's information-security manager sends three questions: what data will go into Claude, which tool will be used, and how outputs are checked before anyone acts on them. What is the MOST effective way to respond?

options.text: Reassure the manager that Claude is built by a safety-focused company, so data handling and output quality are already covered without extra controls.
Send a link to Claude's product homepage and a list of its features, and suggest the manager try it personally to decide whether it is safe.
Ask Claude to write a confident security assessment of itself and forward that to the manager as the formal answer to all three questions.
Answer each question specifically: the data categories involved, the company-approved Claude plan, and who reviews summaries before they are used.

questions.explanation: Security, legal and IT stakeholders need **specifics about this use**: what data goes in, which approved tool and plan is used under company policy, and where a human checks the output. A direct, concrete answer to each question shows the use has been thought through and lets the manager apply the organization's own rules. Generic reassurance or marketing material does not answer what was asked.

whyWrong.A: The vendor's reputation does not answer how this team will handle its data or check outputs. Claude can still be wrong, and data rules come from the organization's policy, not from the brand.
whyWrong.B: Product marketing and a 'try it yourself' suggestion push the work back onto the stakeholder and still say nothing about this team's data, tool choice or review step.
whyWrong.C: A model-written self-assessment is not evidence and may contain confident but wrong statements. The questions are about your team's process, which only you can describe accurately.

questions.mindset: Governance stakeholders need concrete answers about data, tools and review for this specific use.

questions.stem: A customer-support manager is introducing Claude to help agents draft replies to billing questions. Agents will review and edit every draft before sending. At the kickoff meeting, several agents say they are worried this is the first step toward replacing them. Which TWO actions BEST address their concerns while setting accurate expectations? Choose TWO.

options.text: Assure the agents that their jobs are safe and that bringing Claude into the workflow will not change what anyone on the team is responsible for.
Explain concretely what changes in their day (drafting help) and what stays theirs: judging accuracy, tone and the final decision to send.
Tell the agents that Claude's drafts are already reliable enough that their review will only be a formality for the first few weeks.
Avoid discussing the topic further and focus the meeting on how to use the features, since worries usually fade once people try the tool.
Invite agents to help build the review checklist and to log problems they see, so their experience shapes how the process develops.

questions.explanation: Team members need an honest picture of **what changes and what stays their responsibility**, plus a real voice in the process. Explaining that Claude helps with drafting while agents keep judgment and the final send decision is accurate here. Involving them in the review checklist and feedback log treats their expertise as part of the control, which is both true and motivating.

whyWrong.A: No one can honestly guarantee that roles and responsibilities will not change, and if the promise breaks it will damage trust more than the original worry did. Reassurance should be accurate, not blanket.
whyWrong.C: Calling review a formality undermines the very control that catches incorrect or misleading drafts, and it sets the wrong expectation about the agents' responsibility.
whyWrong.D: Ignoring a stated concern rarely makes it go away, and it misses the chance to set clear expectations about roles and accountability.

questions.mindset: Be candid with the team about what changes, what stays theirs, and give them a voice in the controls.

questions.stem: A regional manager asked Claude in a regular chat, without web search or any uploaded files, about the company's travel policy. Claude described rules the company changed two months ago. The manager emails the team lead: 'If it can't get our own policy right, why are we paying for it?' What is the BEST explanation and next step to give the manager?

options.text: Explain that this was a rare one-off glitch, and that asking the same question again a few times will normally give the correct current policy.
Explain that Claude only knows what it was trained on or is given, and that the current policy should be supplied, for example as a Project knowledge file.
Agree that Claude is not suitable for company questions, and recommend that the team stop using it for anything involving internal information.
Explain that a more capable Claude model would already know the company's latest internal policies, so the team should upgrade its model choice.

questions.explanation: Claude does not automatically know an organization's internal documents or recent changes. It works from its training and whatever it is given in the conversation. The honest explanation names that limitation and pairs it with a practical control: give Claude the **current** policy, such as a maintained knowledge file in a Project, and keep checking answers that matter. This preserves the value while fixing the real cause.

whyWrong.A: This misdiagnoses the cause. Claude never had the current policy, so retrying will not fix it and may produce another confident but wrong answer.
whyWrong.C: This abandons useful work when a simple control (supplying the current documents) addresses the issue. Over-caution is also a failure to communicate value accurately.
whyWrong.D: No model knows a company's private, recently changed policies unless they are provided. A bigger model does not solve missing context.

questions.mindset: Name the real limitation (it only knows what it was trained on or given) and pair it with the control.

questions.stem: During a 20-minute demo, Claude impressively turned a messy set of meeting notes into a polished project status report. A member of the leadership team now wants every one of the company's 200 project managers using it for client status reports starting next week, with no other changes. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: Agree to the rollout next week, since the demo showed clearly that Claude handles this task well and delaying would waste the time it can save.
Decline the request, explaining that one demo cannot prove anything and the company should wait until AI tools are reliable enough to use.
Explain that one demo is not evidence of reliability, and propose a short pilot with real projects, a review step and agreed success measures.
Agree to the rollout but ask Claude to add a note to every report saying it may contain errors, so clients know to check it themselves.

questions.explanation: A single, well-chosen demo shows what is **possible**, not what is **reliable** across 200 people, messy real inputs and client audiences. The credible message acknowledges the promise, then proposes a small pilot with real cases, a human review step for client-facing reports and success measures agreed in advance. That turns enthusiasm into evidence without blocking progress.

whyWrong.A: Scaling from one demo to 200 users and external clients, with no review or measurement, sets expectations the evidence cannot support and risks errors reaching clients.
whyWrong.B: Refusing outright ignores the real value the demo suggested. The right response channels interest into a controlled test rather than waiting for perfection.
whyWrong.D: A disclaimer pushes the checking onto clients instead of keeping accountability with the project managers. It does not replace a review step or evidence of reliability.

questions.mindset: A demo shows what's possible; a measured pilot shows what's reliable.

questions.stem: A training coordinator uses Claude to draft course descriptions. Her manager complains: 'I asked it the same thing twice and got two differently worded answers with a different structure. How can we rely on something so inconsistent?' Which TWO responses BEST explain the limitation and how the team will manage it? Choose TWO.

options.text: Explain that wording can vary between runs, and set up shared instructions and a template, for example in a Project, so the structure stays consistent.
Explain that the variation is a defect the vendor will fix soon, so the team should pause its use until answers become identical every time.
Explain that switching to the most capable model will make the answers word-for-word identical whenever the same question is asked.
Explain that a short review checklist for each description confirms required facts and format, regardless of how the wording varies.
Explain that adding 'always answer exactly the same way' to each request guarantees identical output, so no further process is needed.

questions.explanation: Run-to-run variation in wording is normal behavior for a generative model, so the honest answer names it and pairs it with **controls**: shared instructions and a template (for example, Project instructions) to keep structure consistent, and a review checklist so required content is confirmed whatever the phrasing. The manager gets an accurate picture and a reason to trust the process.

whyWrong.B: Describing normal variation as a soon-to-be-fixed defect sets a false expectation and stops useful work for no reason.
whyWrong.C: A more capable model does not guarantee identical wording. This promises a fix that model choice cannot deliver.
whyWrong.E: A prompt instruction cannot guarantee identical output, and promising it would set the manager up for disappointment. Consistency comes from templates plus review, not one sentence.

questions.mindset: Explain variability honestly and point to templates and checklists, not promises of identical output.

questions.stem: A head of compliance at an insurance company has read news stories about AI 'making things up' and proposes banning Claude across the claims department. The claims team had planned to use Claude, in the company-approved workspace, only to draft internal meeting notes and to summarize long internal procedure documents for training. What is the MOST effective response to the head of compliance?

options.text: Explain that the news stories were about other AI products, and that Claude does not make things up when it is used for internal company work.
Accept the ban for now, since the planned uses are not valuable enough to justify pressing the point with compliance this year.
Propose expanding the plan to customer claim decisions as well, to show compliance that Claude's benefits are large enough to justify the risk.
Acknowledge the risk, then show the limited internal scope, the human review step and how errors would be caught, and offer a reviewed trial.

questions.explanation: The concern is legitimate: Claude can produce incorrect or misleading content. The effective response **agrees with the risk** rather than denying it, then shows why this specific use is low-stakes and controlled (internal content, an approved workspace, a named reviewer) and offers a monitored trial. That respects the stakeholder's role and keeps safe, useful work possible.

whyWrong.A: Claiming Claude does not hallucinate is false and would destroy credibility with the compliance team the moment an error appeared.
whyWrong.B: Conceding low-risk, reviewed work without presenting the controls is over-caution. Being unable to defend safe value to a governance stakeholder is itself a communication failure.
whyWrong.C: Expanding into customer claim decisions raises the stakes and moves into a high-risk area that needs qualified human decision-makers. It answers a risk concern by adding risk.

questions.mindset: Agree with the real risk, then show scope and controls that make the use safe.

questions.stem: A procurement analyst is writing a one-page proposal asking the operations director to fund Claude seats for her team for a further quarter. The director is busy, non-technical and has to defend the spend to finance. Which TWO elements will make the proposal MOST persuasive and credible? Choose TWO.

options.text: Results from the team's own trial compared with a baseline, such as time per supplier review before and after, in plain business terms.
A detailed explanation of how large language models are trained, so the director understands the technology behind the results.
The main limitations the team found, each paired with the control it uses, such as checking supplier figures against the source documents.
Published benchmark scores for the latest Claude models, which show how they compare with competing AI systems on standard tests.
A complete list of every Claude feature the team could use in future, so the director sees the full range of what is possible.

questions.explanation: Executives decide on **outcomes, evidence and risk**. The team's own before-and-after results, stated in business terms, show the value in the director's world. Naming the limitations with the controls already in place shows the risk is understood and managed, which makes the case easier to defend to finance. Together they give an honest, decision-ready page.

whyWrong.B: Technical background on model training does not help a non-technical director decide or defend a budget, and it uses up a one-page document.
whyWrong.D: Generic benchmark scores say nothing about this team's work. Stakeholders trust evidence from their own process more than vendor or public test results.
whyWrong.E: A feature list describes possibilities, not outcomes. It makes the proposal longer without showing value or risk for this team.

questions.mindset: Executives need your own evidence in business terms plus honest limits with controls.

questions.stem: A small design agency's contract with a healthcare client requires the agency to disclose any use of AI tools in producing patient-facing materials. The agency now uses Claude to help draft leaflet text, which a writer then edits and a clinician at the client approves. The account manager worries that mentioning AI will make the client nervous. What should the agency do?

options.text: Leave out any mention of AI, since the writer edits every draft heavily and the final wording is therefore entirely the agency's own work.
Disclose the AI use as the contract requires, and explain how drafting help is combined with the writer's edit and the clinician's approval.
Mention AI use only if the client asks about it directly, which satisfies the contract while avoiding an unnecessary conversation.
Stop using Claude for this client entirely, since any disclosure of AI use is likely to damage the relationship with the client.

questions.explanation: The contract sets the rule, so the agency must disclose. Disclosure does not have to be a weakness: explaining how AI drafting help sits inside a process with a professional writer and a **clinician's approval** shows both efficiency and care. For health-related materials, a qualified human review before release is exactly what a careful client expects.

whyWrong.A: Heavy editing does not remove a contractual disclosure requirement. Hiding AI use risks breaching the contract and losing the client's trust if it surfaces later.
whyWrong.C: Waiting to be asked does not meet a requirement to disclose. It treats transparency as optional when the contract makes it mandatory.
whyWrong.D: Abandoning a useful, reviewed process because of an assumed reaction is over-cautious. Honest disclosure with a clear review story usually reassures clients.

questions.mindset: Disclose AI use where contracts or policy expect it, and present the human review as part of the value.

questions.stem: A sales-enablement lead asks Claude to draft an FAQ for regional managers about a new Claude-assisted proposal process. The draft is clear and well organized, but it includes the line 'Claude's answers are 99% accurate' and says proposals 'no longer need legal review for standard terms'. Neither statement came from the lead or the pilot data. What should the lead do before distributing the FAQ?

options.text: Remove both statements, replace them with the pilot's own measured results, and confirm with legal what review rules actually apply.
Keep both statements, since managers respond better to clear numbers, and add a footnote saying figures are approximate estimates.
Ask Claude to double-check its own accuracy figure and keep it if Claude confirms that the number is a reasonable estimate.
Keep the accuracy figure but soften the legal statement to 'may not need legal review', so the FAQ stays encouraging for managers.

questions.explanation: Claude can invent plausible-sounding figures and policy statements. Both lines are **unsupported claims** that would set false expectations: one overstates reliability, the other removes a control without authority. The lead should replace the invented number with real pilot results and confirm the actual review rule with legal, the stakeholder who owns it. Using Claude to draft stakeholder material is fine; the claims in it must be yours and verified.

whyWrong.B: A footnote does not make an invented figure true, and it leaves a statement that removes legal review in place. Managers would act on both.
whyWrong.C: Asking the model to confirm its own number produces more model output, not evidence. The figure has no source in the pilot data.
whyWrong.D: The accuracy figure is still invented, and 'may not need legal review' still signals that a control can be skipped without legal agreeing to that.

questions.mindset: Claude can draft stakeholder messages, but every claim in them must come from your evidence and the real owners.

questions.stem: An HR director, impressed by how quickly Claude summarizes CVs, tells the recruitment team lead: 'Let's have Claude make the final hiring decisions for junior roles. It will remove human bias and save us weeks.' The team lead must respond in a way that keeps the useful part of the idea. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Agree, and ask Claude to explain its reasoning for each hiring decision so that the recruitment team can audit the choices afterwards if needed.
Agree, provided that the CVs are anonymized first, since removing names and photos means the model's decisions can no longer be biased.
Explain that AI can reflect biases too and hiring decisions must stay human, and propose using Claude for summaries against agreed criteria.
Recommend returning to fully manual screening for all roles, since the risks of using AI anywhere in recruitment outweigh the time it saves.

questions.explanation: The director's claim contains a misconception: AI does not automatically remove bias and can reflect biases present in data or instructions. Employment decisions are a high-risk area where a qualified person should make or review the decision. The best response corrects the expectation honestly and **keeps the value**: Claude summarizes CVs against published criteria to save time, and recruiters make and own every decision.

whyWrong.A: An explanation after the fact does not make an automated hiring decision appropriate, and it still hands a decision about people to the model.
whyWrong.B: Anonymizing helps reduce some bias, but it does not make model judgments bias-free or remove the need for human decision-makers in hiring.
whyWrong.D: This discards a genuine, low-risk benefit — summarizing against agreed criteria while recruiters keep the decisions. The evidence points to narrowing the use, not abandoning it.

questions.mindset: Correct the 'AI removes bias' myth, keep decisions about people human, and keep the time-saving part.

questions.stem: A finance team piloted Claude for drafting responses to supplier payment queries. Results were mixed: simple status queries were drafted in a fraction of the usual time with few edits, while disputed-invoice queries needed so much rework that they took about as long as writing from scratch. The finance controller asks for a single verdict: 'Did it work or not?' What is the MOST useful way to report the results?

options.text: Report the overall average time saved across all query types, since one combined number is simpler for the controller to understand and act on.
Report that the pilot failed, because a tool that cannot handle the harder disputed queries is not reliable enough for the finance team.
Report only the results for simple queries, since those show the tool's real potential and the disputed queries can be fixed later.
Break the results down by query type and recommend using Claude for simple queries while disputed ones stay manual for now.

questions.explanation: A single verdict would hide the most useful finding: **where** Claude adds value and where it does not. Segmenting the results lets the controller make a precise decision: adopt it for simple status queries, keep disputed-invoice queries manual, and perhaps revisit them later. This is honest about the limitation and still captures the value the pilot demonstrated.

whyWrong.A: A blended average masks that one category gained a lot and the other gained nothing. The controller could then expand use into the very cases where it does not help.
whyWrong.B: Calling the whole pilot a failure throws away a clear win on simple queries. The evidence supports a narrower scope, not abandonment.
whyWrong.C: Leaving out the disputed-query results hides a limitation the controller needs to know about. Selective reporting undermines trust in every later update.

questions.mindset: Mixed results usually mean 'use it here, not there'; report the split honestly.

questions.stem: An accounting firm uses Claude to help draft sections of the management letters it sends to audit clients. A client's finance director asks the engagement partner: 'If something in this letter is wrong because the AI made a mistake, who is responsible?' Which TWO points should the partner include in the answer? Choose TWO.

options.text: Responsibility is shared with the AI vendor, since the tool produced the draft text and the firm only reviewed and formatted it for the client.
The firm remains fully responsible for the letter, and a named professional on the engagement signs off on its content before it is issued.
AI-drafted sections are generally more accurate than human-written ones, so the chance of an error in the letter is negligible in practice.
Every factual statement and figure in the letter is checked against the audit working papers by the team before the partner approves it.
The client should review the AI-drafted sections carefully, since the firm cannot be held accountable for content a model has generated.

questions.explanation: Accountability cannot be delegated to a tool. The honest answer states plainly that the **firm and a named professional** own the letter, and it describes the **verification step** that makes that ownership meaningful: facts and figures are checked against the working papers before approval. This reassures the client with truth rather than with claims about the AI's accuracy.

whyWrong.A: Pointing to the vendor shifts accountability away from the professionals who issue the letter. The firm signs it, so the firm owns it.
whyWrong.C: This overstates the tool's reliability. Claude can produce incorrect content, which is exactly why verification is needed.
whyWrong.E: Pushing the checking onto the client reverses the professional relationship and abandons accountability for the firm's own deliverable.

questions.mindset: A named human owns every deliverable; describe the check that backs that ownership.

questions.stem: A logistics coordinator has 60 seconds at the start of a meeting with the chief operating officer to explain why her team's Claude trial is worth continuing. The COO is non-technical and cares about service levels. Which opening statement is MOST effective?

options.text: 'Over four weeks, customer delay notices went out in 20 minutes instead of 2 hours, and our dispatcher checked each one before it was sent.'
'We used Claude's Projects, Artifacts and connectors together, which is the most advanced setup available on our current plan.'
'AI is transforming logistics everywhere, and if we don't adopt it fully this year our competitors will leave us far behind.'
'Claude is a large language model with a very large context window, so it can process much more information than our team can.'

questions.explanation: Stakeholders care about **outcomes**, not features. The strongest opening ties the trial to the COO's priority (service levels) with a concrete before-and-after result, and in the same breath shows the human check that keeps it safe. It is short, specific and believable.

whyWrong.B: A list of features tells a non-technical executive nothing about service levels or outcomes. It describes tools, not value.
whyWrong.C: Sweeping hype with no evidence sounds like a sales pitch and invites skepticism. It also pushes for full adoption that the trial does not justify.
whyWrong.D: Technical capability claims are not business results. The COO needs to know what improved for customers, not how the model works.

questions.mindset: Lead with a measured business outcome the stakeholder cares about, plus the human check.
